author: Attributed to the scholar Veylin of the Eastern College

#The Singing Halls

Those who have entered the deeper Dwemer ruins often speak of a hum that seems to come from the walls themselves, felt in the teeth more than heard by the ears. I have spent many years trying to understand it.

#Tone and Stone

The Dwemer seem to have believed that every material has a voice, a particular note at which it trembles most freely. Their doors are opened not by keys but by sequences of tones struck on small bells or rods set into the walls.

I have opened four such doors by patient experiment. The fifth answered my experiments with a jet of steam, which is why my eyebrows are a different colour from my hair.

#The Great Resonators

In the central halls of the largest ruins stand towering structures of brass and crystal. When struck, they sing a note so deep that dust falls from the ceiling. I believe they were used to tune the entire city, as a bard tunes a lute.

What tune the Dwemer were trying to play, and for what audience, I cannot guess.

#A Warning

Resonance is not merely sound. A note struck in the right place can crack stone, shatter glass and wake things that were sleeping. More than one explorer has struck a resonator out of curiosity and brought the ceiling down, or woke every automaton in the hall at once.

Listen before you strike. The Dwemer certainly did.
